newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Clinton to hail U.S. role in rebuilding Europe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to hail U.S. role in rebuilding Europe.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, fresh from signing an historic deal linking Cold War enemies NATO and Russia, will hail another success story on Wednesday -- the rebuilding of Western Europe.

Clinton flew into the Dutch seat of government late on Tuesday to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan, the U.S.-funded programme that was launched in June 1947 to help raise Europe out of the ashes of World War Two.

Against a backdrop of the Netherlands' rich mix of medieval history and modern booming economy, Clinton is expected to urge the incorporation of the former Communist bloc into Western Europe's main institutions, NATO and the European Union.
He will meet leaders of the 15-nation EU -- itself created to stop the continent's nations fram warring with each other -- in the twice-yearly EU-U.S. summit.
But foreign policy questions and colourful celebrations aside, the American president is likely to be dogged by questions about the Paula Jones sexual harassment case.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Tuesday that the U.S. Constitution does not require a lawsuit brought by Jones against Clinton to be delayed until he leaves office in 2001.

The ruling cast a pall for the White House over what was otherwise a day of triumph, the signing in Paris of an accord between NATO and Moscow on a new security relationship that will clear the way for the alliance to expand eastwards without triggering renewed East-West tensions.
Clinton said the pact realised the long-sought goal of "a peaceful, democratic, undivided Europe".
His visit to the Netherlands, the current EU president, will include a formal lunch with Dutch Queen Beatrix and leaders from across the continent to celebrate the anniversary of the Marshall Plan.
Clinton will later unveil a statue of General George Marshall in Rotterdam, a port city that was devastated by bombing during the war.
The working part of the visit will consist of a two-hour meeting on Wednesday morning between Clinton, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer.
U.S. officials have played down the chances of any rifts appearing between the two sides during the meeting, noting that transatlantic relations are warmer now than they have been for some time.
Part of this is because a row over America's anti-Cuba Helms-Burton law, which the EU sees as a threat to its businesses, has been defused.
The EU has also adopted a more distant approach to Iran -- to the delight of the White House -- since a German court found Tehran to be involved in the murder of Kurdish Iranian opposition leaders.
The U.S.-EU talks will culminate in the signing of two agreements -- on customs and on common controls on trade in chemical ingredients that can be used to make narcotics.
Foreign policy discussions were set to range from North Korea's nuclear programme, to struggling Middle East peace talks, Bosnia and Africa's Great Lakes region.
